doc.title: David Spinozza interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, NY, September 27, 2025

title: Happy accidents: an R&B guitarist turned chameleon
summary: Spinozza says he was a rhythm and blues player who learned to arrange for his horn bands. They touch on Howard Johnson and John Lennon's thoughts on horn players.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Yeah. I was lucky enough to hear you play last night and we’ll talk about that, but I’m going to quote you, this is just from like a half an hour ago at breakfast.
You’re a very quotable guy, and you said, “I’m a quick learner and a quick forgetter.”

Remember you said that? And in the brief time you were sort of describing your career I realized that you’ve been the recipient of some moments that you didn’t necessarily cause to happen but like happy accidents?

I would say, yes, yes. Probably because when I came up I was a rhythm & blues guitar player basically. I wouldn’t – I never really considered myself a jazz guitarist. Because I certainly listened to a lot of jazz players: Wes Montgomery, Joe Pass, people like that, you know, Chuck Wayne. I knew all these guitarists. I knew who they were. But I was mostly playing rhythm & blues. I had horn bands and I learned to arrange because the horns would say, “Well what do we play?” And I started to figure out how to write for horns and stuff like that. So I became kind of a chameleon in the music business. And that’s how I got started.
You know you just gave me a flash because I was able to interview Howard Johnson.
Oh sure. I know him well.
And he talked about getting a call to play a John Lennon session, which I know you had done.
But it might have been before. At any rate John Lennon just had this thought that when you get in professional horn players that something magic just happens. Like they know what to do.
Like they know what parts to play.
